{{short description|American mathematician (1930–2000)}}
'''Franklin Paul Peterson''' (1930–2000) was an American [[mathematician]] specializing in [[algebraic topology]]. He was a professor of mathematics at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name="tech">{{citation|title=Franklin P. Peterson|journal=The Tech|volume=120|issue=41|date=September 12, 2000|url=http://tech.mit.edu/V120/N41/petersonobit.41n.html|access-date=October 19, 2013|archive-date=October 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191030054523/http://tech.mit.edu/V120/N41/petersonobit.41n.html|url-status=dead}}.</ref><ref name="nams">{{citation|title=Franklin P. Peterson (1930–2000)|journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]|
first1=Edgar H.|last1=Brown|author-link1=Edgar H. Brown| 
first2=Frederick R.|last2=Cohen|
first3=Frederick W.|last3=Gehring|author-link3= Frederick Gehring |
first4=Haynes R.|last4=Miller| author-link4=Haynes Miller |
first5=B. Alan|last5=Taylor|
url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200110/fea-peterson.pdf|date=November 2001|volume=48|issue=10|pages=1161–1168|mr=1861657}}.</ref>

==Life and career==
Peterson was born in [[Aurora, Illinois]], on August 27, 1930, the older of two brothers. His father died when he was young, and he was raised by his mother and uncle.<ref name="nams"/> He attended [[Northwestern University]], graduating in 1952, and earned his [[Ph.D.]] in 1955 from [[Princeton University]] under the supervision of [[Norman Steenrod]].<ref name="tech"/><ref name="nams"/><ref name="mg">{{mathgenealogy|name=Franklin Paul Peterson|id=8592}}</ref> After postdoctoral studies at Princeton, he joined the MIT faculty in 1958.<ref name="tech"/><ref name="nams"/>

Peterson edited the ''[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]]'' from 1966 to 1970.<ref name="tech"/> He also served for many years as treasurer of the AMS; in that role he played a key role in resolving tensions between the dual directors of the society as it was then structured, and worked to build up a large reserve fund for the society.<ref name="tech"/><ref name="nams"/>

Peterson married Marilyn Rutz in 1959.<ref name="nams"/>
He died of a stroke on September 1, 2000, near [[Washington, DC]].<ref name="tech"/><ref name="nams"/>

==Contributions==
Peterson's early research used [[cohomology]] to study [[homotopy|homotopy equivalence]]. Later, he did important work on the properties of [[loop space]]s.<ref name="nams"/>

The [[Peterson–Stein formula]] is named after him, after he wrote about it with Norman Stein in 1960. He also introduced the [[Brown–Peterson cohomology]] with [[Edgar H. Brown]] in 1966.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Wilson | first = W. Stephen |author-link=W. Stephen Wilson
 | isbn = 9780821816998
 | location = Washington, D.C.
 | mr = 655040
 | publisher = Conference Board of the Mathematical Sciences
 | series = CBMS Regional Conference Series in Mathematics
 | title = Brown-Peterson homology: an introduction and sampler
 | volume = 48
 | year = 1982}}.</ref>
 
He advised over 20 doctoral students (different sources give different numbers, in part because Robert E. Mosher, whom Peterson considered his first student, had a different official advisor) and has over 100 academic descendants.<ref name="tech"/><ref name="nams"/><ref name="mg"/>
